title: Anime And Fangame RPG Maker Games and RPG Maker 2003

posts.author: A_Higher_Plane
posts.body:
So, what do you guys think about the anime RPG Maker games? They're illegal, aren't they? I enjoyed the 2024 RPG Maker MZ anime game Dragon Ball: Goku's Tale. I also enjoyed that old popular Naruto game made by RPG Maker 2003.
There were so many anime RPG Maker 2003 games like Saint Seiya ones, this Naruto one, and a Dragon Ball one. Why is RPG Maker 2003 so famous for creating anime games? It seems that some still use it in 2024.
Would creating a fangame (not just anime but other IPs like Mario, Harry Potter, Star Wars, etc.) be more fun than an original game? But they're illegal.

posts.author: Andar
posts.body:
fangames are easier to make because the world already exists - it takes a lot of work to build a new world from scratch and invent a consistent background, and that work is rarely seen directly in games.
fangames are also easier to attach to and find, because someone else already spent the time or money (or both) to bring out their names publically. Most people can't put in the effort to make a new game known around the world if they have no one or nothing to attach to. Which is the main reason why such games are illegal, you try to latch on someones past advertising cost without paying for that privilege.
For truly creative people with enough time it is usually more fun to develop their own worlds, despite that including a lot of less fun parts like collecting names and so on.
But if you aren't as creative or not willing to spend extra weeks on background work, then it is easier to attach to an existing world.

posts.author: TG22
posts.body:
Two reasons why fan games are usually fun to play, in my humble opinion :
The fan who is making them is usually breaking some of the rules that the original author is inflicting to themselves, so in fan-made games you can see the characters you like, the world you like, under a new light.
Many official games made with strong licenses have all their budget spent... on buying the license. Then the gameplay, story, and even sometimes the graphics are underfinanced, making them dull, boring, and make you regret you bought the game (but they don't care, they know you will buy the next one anyway). That's when fan-made games can make some contrast.
But none of these reasons make them legal.

It depends on the specific wishes of the person of course, but it is very easy to see with fanfiction (which is easier to produce than fangames).
While there are a lot of very good fanfictions with interesting stories, there are also several different groups of fanfiction that show a tendency that would never happen in the original stories - like making the main characters overpowered to just clear all opposition (good authors and especially game developers make the enemies a challenge), or turning the original group into a harem, or mixing two or more different franchises as crossover (which no original creator can do without a lot of negotiation) and so on.
no, not everyone reads those stories - but given the millions of people there are more than enough to be interested.

The rules I'm talking about are not intrinsicly "good" or "bad" to remove. They are just untold - sometimes unconscious - rules that depend on the original author of each fiction.
A fan of the fiction will be able to detect them, and play with them in a fan fiction. And this will please some of the other fans.
For example you have authors with rules like "this character will never lose hope", "this character will never ask for help", "this character will never be in a ridiculous situation" etc...

posts.author: Kyuubits
posts.body:
I actually made a short fan fiction game 2 weeks ago of one of my favorite animes from the 80s called Legend of the Galactic Heroes.
It was for the Brackeys game jam (I ranked 42 out 1500 games
).
It is not always illegal:
Fanfiction will not be held liable for copyright infringement if it falls under the fair use defense. In determining the applicability of the fair use defense to a secondary use such as fanfiction, courts consider the following four factors:
"the purpose and character of the use, including whether such use is of a commercial nature or is for nonprofit educational purposes;
the nature of the copyrighted work;
the amount and substantiality of the portion used in relation to the copyrighted work as a whole; and
the effect of the use upon the potential market for or value of the copyrighted work."
[8]
Click to expand...
This is only a tiny part taken from the
wikipedia page
about the subject, which is a good read of you are interested in the legal side of this topic.
There are many reasons that I chose to do this:
- I was rewatching it and felt I wanted to contribute to amazing philosophical and moral discussions that the story explored.
- I wanted to express my love and appreciation for the original material. It's a special way to visit a place you want to got to.
- Being a solo developer, doing almost everything from scratch including Pixel art and animation, music and writing, in a super short time frame of a game jam (one week in this case), it was very helpful to have an already existing world to house my work and gave me the freedom to focus on these other aspects of game development.
- I wanted to design my very own spaceship in the aesthetic of the show because they have amazing style.
- It is a great way to learn from a work you admire, by taking it apart and analyzing what give it a unique identity
- It can introduce people to an ip that they had never heard of before; many of my friends are now watching the anime because of my game. It is why the Manga industry in Japan tolerates such a wide spread of Doujinshi: free advertising.
...
There are many useful reasons.
I usually do original works, and love world building. It is usually the part I spend the most of my time on because i enjoy it so much. So it is good from time to time to use a pre-made world so you can focus on improving your other skills.
If you're interested in taking a look at the game I'm talking about, you can check it out
here
on itch.

posts.author: TheAM-Dol
posts.body:
TG22 said:
Many official games made with strong licenses have all their budget spent... on buying the license
Click to expand...
This is a false equivalency.
So when it comes to license games, there are just as many good licensed games as there are bad.
Usually the quality has more to do with the terms of the license and the competency of the development team.
A good recent example of a license game would be:
Space Marine 2.
Or, how about any of the lego games?
There have been many contracted games, which we generally also call licensed games sometimes, but in these cases they are games made by studios to release a game to coincide with the release of another more major release...usually a movie, 9 times out of 10. These games often suck because the studios contracted have limited experience and often limited time.
Basically, the short of it is: Commercial or not has nothing to do with the quality.
Now, more
quantity
of fan games may increase the chances of a good game.
Doing things through the legal channels will result in fewer people taking on that franchise, resulting in fewer releases. So when a release in that franchise misses, well...it may be awhile until we see a good one.
However all the fan game devs of, say Star Wars, don't negotiate a license with the House of Mouse. They just make the game they want. But trust me, most of them are not very good and just fade in obscurity. But with countless people making their own take on the Stars World, one of them is bound to be pretty interesting.
I'd argue the ratio of good games to bad games is probably higher in the commercially licensed space than in realm of fan games.

while your quote is completely correct, it misses one important point:
for a court to consider fair use, you already have to be in court (that means have paid for a lawyer), and there is no guarantee that the court follows your argumentation.
most people who do fangames are not able or willing to pay a lawyer upfront in the hope to be reimbursed after the court rules in their favor.
at the moment the only way to guarantee fair use without being in court is to make a parody of the original, that means ridicule and laugh at the game you're a fan of....

I am a comic book artist and I got sued by my very oppressive government for "inciting civil unrest" in a story I published ten years ago. I hired a lawyer after, who actually took the case for free because it is a cause he believes in personally. I don't hire a lawyer every time i draw or publish a comic book.
